author: Datman94
quote:
Marvel’s Wolverine is the most fun I’ve had with a video game in three years, since Insomniac’s Spider-Man 2. Having now completed it, I genuinely consider it a masterpiece, which is why some of the lukewarm reviews have left me scratching my head.

Everyone is entitled to their opinion, and no game is above criticism. But what frustrates me is how inconsistently certain standards seem to be applied. Some of the things people criticize Wolverine for are the exact same things they praise or completely overlook in other critically acclaimed games.

Let's talk about the length first.

One of the biggest complaints I've seen is that Wolverine is too short for a full-priced AAA game. But since when did a game's length determine its quality?

Titanfall 2, Resident Evil 4, BioShock Infinite, Dead Space Remake, DOOM Eternal, Uncharted 4, Detroit: Become Human, Jedi: Fallen Order, and God of War (2018) all offer relatively focused single-player experiences. Their campaigns vary in length, but several can be completed in roughly 10–20 hours.

Yet these games are celebrated as some of the best of their respective generations.

God of War's main story is generally around 20 hours, depending on how you play. It was a full-priced AAA release, and its length didn't stop it from receiving widespread acclaim.

I'm not saying all these games are exactly the same length as Wolverine. I'm saying we've spent years celebrating focused, cinematic single-player games, so why is that suddenly a major problem here?

I'd rather have 15 hours of incredible gameplay than 50 hours of repetitive filler. More content doesn't automatically mean better content.

And speaking of God of War, let's talk about the gameplay complaints.

I've seen people criticize Wolverine for being linear, telling you where to go, and occasionally holding your hand.

Have we forgotten how often Atreus tells Kratos exactly what to do? How many times does he point out a puzzle solution before you've even had a chance to figure it out?

God of War and Ragnarök have both received criticism for excessive companion hints, yet that didn't prevent people from recognizing how incredible those games are.

And rightly so!

But why is a similar design choice a relatively minor annoyance in one game and a serious problem in another?

The same goes for linearity. Uncharted 4 is linear. The Last of Us is linear. God of War has plenty of linear sections.

Not every game needs to be an open world. Sometimes a tightly constructed experience with deliberate pacing is exactly what makes a game great.

Now, the combat. This is where I disagree with some reviewers the most.

Wolverine's combat is SO much better than I think some people are giving it credit for.

There's a massive difference between getting through a combat encounter and actually mastering the mechanics.

Once you start experimenting with abilities, learning combinations, and understanding how everything works together, the combat becomes incredibly satisfying.

You can beat God of War without mastering its combat system, too. That doesn't mean the depth isn't there.

I'm not saying Wolverine and God of War have identical combat systems. I'm saying Wolverine deserves to be judged on what its combat can actually do when someone takes the time to learn it.

The brutality, speed, impact, and overall intensity are fantastic. it makes you FEEL like Wolverine. Yes said it.
Thats something Insomniac has always understood about superhero games. Spider-Man makes you feel like Spider-Man, and Wolverine delivers that same sense of character identity.

And the boss fights? Some of the most fun I've had in years. The spectacle, intensity, and satisfaction of overcoming them genuinely reminded me of the excitement I get from God of War and Souls games.

Not because they're mechanically identical, but because they deliver that same feeling of accomplishment.

Another thing: wanting more from a game doesn't mean what we got was bad.

Would I have loved to play as Jean Grey? Absolutely. Especially after seeing what was included in the leaked 2023 development material.

Would I have loved even more content? Of course!

But I gave Spider-Man 2 a 10/10, and I STILL wish we could freely roam New York as Venom.

Does that mean Spider-Man 2 suddenly deserves an 8 because it didn't include something I wanted? Of course not.

There's a difference between a game failing to deliver what it promises and a game simply not including every feature you personally hoped for.

If we judged every game against an imaginary version containing everything we could possibly want, practically nothing would ever deserve a 10.

And that brings me to something else.

A 10/10 doesn't mean a game is literally flawless.

God of War isn't flawless. Spider-Man 2 isn't flawless. Resident Evil 4 isn't flawless.

No game is.

A perfect score means the overall experience was exceptional enough that its shortcomings didn't meaningfully diminish your enjoyment.
